Storyline 1: Full releases declined. Where did the change occur?¶

This notebook starts with a question: When a request is closed, how has the outcome for the requester changed over time?

We begin with government-wide outcomes, identify the agencies that shape the government-wide curve, and then decide which pattern supports a distinct story. The sequence reconstructs the documented exploration and explains the reasoning behind each analytical step.

One point applies to all four storylines. DHS's share of dispositions (DHS's closed requests divided by all closed requests) was 18.9% in FY2008 and 60.8% in FY2025, so government-wide FOIA rates increasingly reflect DHS's own rates. Each storyline therefore shows DHS, or a group of immigration-related units, next to the rest before drawing a conclusion: this notebook in Section 2, Storyline 3 for appeal outcomes, and Storyline 4 for backlog, where three of the four separated units are in DHS. The opening storyline, Storyline 0, explains why.

The finding in one sentence (Section 8): outside DHS and NARA, full releases fell from 50.0% of dispositions in FY2008 to 21.4% in FY2025; the decline remains after removing any single agency or component, and it comes mainly from agencies' own full-release shares falling, not from a shift in which agencies handle requests. Within that fall, in FY2017–25 without VBA most reflects more requests closed without records being processed (8.74 of 12.74 points); among requests whose records were reviewed, the full-release share also fell, but by less (54.7% to 48.1%).

Roadmap: what each section asks and finds. All shares are percentages of each year's dispositions.

Section Question Finding
1 How did government-wide outcomes change? Full release fell sharply while partial release and no records rose; the single government-wide figure does not show who changed
2 How much of the government-wide curve is DHS? A large part of the government-wide fall is DHS's growing weight; outside DHS the share also fell, so the notebook follows outside DHS
3 Why does the outside-DHS curve still swing? NARA's outcome categories swap every few years; it is set aside, and the population becomes outside DHS and NARA
4 Outside DHS and NARA, how did the four outcomes change? Provisionally: full release down, partial release up, no records roughly flat
5 Where does the jump in partial releases from FY2023 come from? VBA, so the partial-release rise must be told in two periods; on the reviewed-requests denominator, most of agencies' own FY2017–25 fall (without VBA) reflects more requests closed without records being processed
6 Did agencies' own shares fall, or did the mix of agencies change? Mainly agencies' own shares, not a shift in which agencies handle requests; most agencies fell
7 Does the finding depend on any single unit or on the list of agencies? Only the FY2017–25 partial-release rise depends on VBA; EOIR pulls the other way; the changing list of agencies does not matter
8 The resulting story One sentence, five points, what not to say, leads to follow up, and methods limits
Appendix Where does the rise in DHS no-records outcomes come from? Mainly CBP and USCIS

Terms: "points" and "pp" both mean percentage points, the difference between two percentages. In Section 2 an outcome's "rate" is its share of a group's dispositions, the same thing called a "share" elsewhere; a group's share of all dispositions is its "weight" (Section 2 calls it "DHS's share of dispositions"). An agency is a department or independent agency; a component is a unit within an agency that reports separately; an agency without components counts as one unit.

1. Start with dispositions: which outcomes are changing?¶

Table 02 records how requests were closed. Full release, partial release, no records, and full denial based on exemptions are distinct outcomes. Viewing them together reveals what else changed as the full-release share declined.

Definitions (DOJ Annual FOIA Report Handbook, 2019):

Disposition Meaning Key point for reading the data
Full release All responsive records are released in full. Nothing is withheld.
Partial release Some, but not all, of the requested information is released. Usually exemptions were applied, but not always: if part is released and the rest is not found, or is referred to another agency, the request also counts here.
No records The agency tells the requester it has no responsive records. Nothing was found for the whole request. If part was found and released, it is a partial release.
Full exemption denial All requested information is withheld under FOIA exemptions. Also includes “neither confirm nor deny” responses.

Each closed request has exactly one disposition. If any record was reviewed, the request must be reported as full release, partial release or full exemption denial; no records and the other eight categories apply only when no record was processed.

The source is the November 6 API component master. Every year's denominator is the sum of the 12 disposition categories. Agency totals are not added to their own components. The chart shows the four outcomes this storyline follows, so its lines do not sum to 100%. The other eight categories are not plotted but remain in the denominator; the second table below lists them: referred to another agency or component, withdrawn by the requester, fee-related reason, records not reasonably described, improper request for other reason, not an agency record, duplicate request, and other reason. Together they account for 21.6% of dispositions in FY2008 and 19.8% in FY2025, and the four plotted outcomes account for the remaining 78.4% and 80.2%. Section 4 groups these eight as “other dispositions.”

The government-wide full-release share trends downward over the long run, but the curve is uneven. Over the same period the partial-release share rises, and the no-records share also rises overall, with a sharp drop in FY2018. This raises the next question: Does the government-wide curve reflect a shared pattern across agencies, or changes in a few agencies with many requests or unusual outcomes?

Start with DHS, which earlier project analysis identified as closing a very large number of requests. Comparing three lines—all government, DHS, and outside DHS—tests whether one government-wide summary is sufficient.

2. Separate DHS: what does the government-wide figure combine?¶

Step 1: Split the government-wide figures into DHS and outside DHS¶

“Outside DHS” means all agencies and components other than DHS.

DHS differs from agencies outside DHS in all four outcomes (each share below is a percentage of that group's own dispositions). In every year, DHS has a lower full-release share (2.4%–12.1%) and a lower full-exemption-denial share (0.4%–2.7%) than agencies outside DHS, and a higher partial-release share (40.0%–62.2%). DHS's no-records share rises from 7.9% in FY2008 to 40.2% in FY2025, when the share outside DHS is 13.4%. DHS's share of dispositions also grows, from 18.9% in FY2008 to 60.8% in FY2025, so DHS weighs more heavily on the government-wide curves over time. Because each government-wide share is an average of DHS and outside DHS weighted by their dispositions, it sits closer to whichever of the two, DHS or outside DHS, accounts for more than half of dispositions. DHS stays below half through FY2019 (49.0% that year), when the government-wide line is closer to the outside-DHS line; from FY2020, DHS exceeds half and the government-wide line is closer to the DHS line in all four panels. For example, the government-wide partial-release share rises from 17.8% in FY2008 to 37.7% in FY2025; over the same years the share outside DHS rises from 10.0% to 34.3%, while DHS's own share falls from 51.3% to 40.0% (it peaked at 62.2% in FY2015). A single government-wide account would combine different changes.

The same numbers can also be read the other way: one chart each for all government, DHS and outside DHS, with all four outcomes in each chart. This view shows which outcome is most common within each population, and when that changes. The three charts share the same vertical scale. The first (all government) repeats the Section 1 data, placed here for side-by-side comparison.

def runs(sr):
    # consecutive years with the same largest outcome, e.g. 'FY2008–13: Full release'
    out,start=[],sr.index[0]
    for prev,y in zip(list(sr.index[:-1])+[sr.index[-1]],list(sr.index[1:])+[None]):
        if y is None or sr[y]!=sr[prev]:
            out.append(f'FY{start}–{str(prev)[2:]}: {sr[prev]}' if start!=prev else f'FY{prev}: {sr[prev]}'); start=y
    return '; '.join(out)
print('Most common of the four outcomes, by year')
for s,m in mix_by_scope.items(): print(f'  {s}: {runs(m.idxmax(axis=1))}')

# Checks for the statements below

What the three charts show

  • All government: full release is the most common outcome in FY2008–13; partial release is the most common in every year from FY2014. No records exceeds full release in FY2017 and in every year from FY2021.
  • DHS: partial release is the most common outcome in every year from FY2008 to FY2024. In FY2025, no records (40.2%) edges past partial release (40.0%). No records exceeds full release in every year from FY2013.
  • Outside DHS: full release is the most common outcome in FY2008–22; partial release is the most common in FY2023–25. No records never exceeds full release.
  • The FY2017–18 jump outside DHS: full release jumps from 33.2% to 43.4% and no records falls from 24.4% to 12.6%. Without NARA most of the jump disappears: full release rises only 2.1 points (38.0% to 40.1%), and no records is 13.6% in both years. Section 3 examines NARA.

The government-wide switch from full to partial release as the most common outcome therefore comes nine years before the switch outside DHS, because the government-wide figure includes DHS, where partial release was the most common outcome through FY2024. The switch outside DHS depends on VBA, which Section 5 examines.

Step 2: Split the change in the government-wide share into two parts¶

Why split it:

  • The government-wide full-release share depends on two things: the full-release rates of DHS and of agencies outside DHS, and DHS's share of dispositions, that is, how much of all dispositions DHS closes.
  • Both changed between FY2008 and FY2025: DHS's full-release rate fell from 11.4% to 2.4% and the rate outside DHS from 48.7% to 20.7%, while DHS's share of dispositions rose from 18.9% to 60.8%.
  • The government-wide full-release share fell 32.1 points (41.6% to 9.5%). The government-wide figure alone cannot show how much of this is agencies releasing in full less often and how much is more requests going to DHS, which rarely releases in full.
  • This step separates the two and measures each in percentage points. It is not a test of whether DHS's own full-release rate rose or fell; that can be read directly from DHS's rate, which fell.
  • The method is a decomposition of a difference between two rates (Kitagawa 1955): it splits the change in the government-wide share into parts that add up exactly to the total. It is an arithmetic split, a descriptive tool rather than a statistical model or inference, and it does not explain causes.

A made-up example explains the method first; the real data follow.

(a) The idea (the numbers in this example are made up)

Suppose there are only two agencies: A (like DHS, rarely releases in full) and B (like agencies outside DHS, often releases in full). Between year 1 and year 2, two things happen: B's full-release rate falls from 50% to 30%, and 40 requests move from B to A. Go from year 1 to year 2 in two steps, changing one thing at a time (bold cells are the ones that change):

A requests A rate B requests B rate Full releases Government-wide
Year 1 actual 20 10% 80 50% 2 + 40 = 42 42%
Hypothetical 20 10% 80 30% 2 + 24 = 26 26%
Year 2 actual 60 10% 40 30% 6 + 12 = 18 18%
  • Row 1 to row 2 (42% to 26%): the request counts stay fixed and only the rates change. These 16 points are the effect of A's and B's own rates falling; A did not change, so all of it comes from B: 80 × (50% − 30%) = 16.
  • Row 2 to row 3 (26% to 18%): the rates stay fixed and only the request counts change. The 40 requests that moved would give 40 × 30% = 12 full releases at B but give 40 × 10% = 4 at A, so 8 fewer. These 8 points are the effect of A's larger share of requests (20% to 60%).
  • Row 2 is hypothetical and never happened: it combines year 1's request counts with year 2's rates. Demographers call such a figure a standardized rate (as in age-standardized death rates). Its only purpose is to separate the two changes; it does not predict what would have happened had A not grown, but simply recombines one year's rates with another year's request counts.

(b) The real data

Start with the real counts. The government-wide full-release share = (DHS full releases + full releases outside DHS) ÷ (DHS dispositions + dispositions outside DHS). Each year has one table in the same order as the formula, with the sum in the last row; below each table the numbers are plugged into the formula.

In [4]:
# (a) Counts: government-wide rate = total full releases / total dispositions
def counts(y,base):
    disp=sum(tot(G,c,y,base) for c in c02); fr=tot(G,FG,y,base)
    return {'Dispositions':disp,'Full releases':fr,'Full release (%)':100*fr/disp}
cnt=pd.DataFrame({(y,s):counts(y,b) for y in (2008,2025) for s,b in scopes}).T
cnt['Share of all dispositions (%)']=[100*cnt.loc[(y,s),'Dispositions']/cnt.loc[(y,'All government'),'Dispositions'] for y,s in cnt.index]
# One table per year, in the order of the formula: numerator, denominator, share; the parts first, then their sum
cols=['Full releases','Dispositions','Full release (%)','Share of all dispositions (%)']
fmt={'Full releases':'{:,.0f}','Dispositions':'{:,.0f}','Full release (%)':'{:.1f}','Share of all dispositions (%)':'{:.1f}'}
for y in (2008,2025):
    d,o,a=cnt.loc[(y,'DHS')],cnt.loc[(y,'Outside DHS')],cnt.loc[(y,'All government')]
    assert d['Full releases']+o['Full releases']==a['Full releases'] and d['Dispositions']+o['Dispositions']==a['Dispositions']
    print(f'FY{y}')
    display(cnt.loc[y].loc[['DHS','Outside DHS','All government'],cols].rename(index={'All government':'All government (= DHS + outside DHS)'}).style.format(fmt))
    print(f"Full-release share = ({d['Full releases']:,.0f} + {o['Full releases']:,.0f}) ÷ ({d['Dispositions']:,.0f} + {o['Dispositions']:,.0f})"
          f" = {a['Full releases']:,.0f} ÷ {a['Dispositions']:,.0f} = {a['Full release (%)']:.1f}%\n")
assert cnt['Dispositions'].astype(int).tolist()==[578141,109028,469113,1635173,994992,640181]
assert cnt['Full releases'].astype(int).tolist()==[240667,12405,228262,155909,23414,132495]
assert cnt['Full release (%)'].round(1).tolist()==[41.6,11.4,48.7,9.5,2.4,20.7]
assert cnt['Share of all dispositions (%)'].round(1).tolist()==[100.0,18.9,81.1,100.0,60.8,39.2]
assert round(cnt.loc[(2025,'DHS'),'Dispositions']/cnt.loc[(2008,'DHS'),'Dispositions'],1)==9.1

FY2008
  Full releases Dispositions Full release (%) Share of all dispositions (%)
DHS 12,405 109,028 11.4 18.9
Outside DHS 228,262 469,113 48.7 81.1
All government (= DHS + outside DHS) 240,667 578,141 41.6 100.0 
Full-release share = (12,405 + 228,262) ÷ (109,028 + 469,113) = 240,667 ÷ 578,141 = 41.6%

FY2025
  Full releases Dispositions Full release (%) Share of all dispositions (%)
DHS 23,414 994,992 2.4 60.8
Outside DHS 132,495 640,181 20.7 39.2
All government (= DHS + outside DHS) 155,909 1,635,173 9.5 100.0 
Full-release share = (23,414 + 132,495) ÷ (994,992 + 640,181) = 155,909 ÷ 1,635,173 = 9.5%

In FY2008, DHS closed about 109,000 requests, 18.9% of all dispositions. In FY2025 it closed about 995,000, more than nine times as many, and 60.8% of all dispositions. Outside DHS, dispositions grew only from about 469,000 to about 640,000.

To match the example, convert counts to “per 100 dispositions” (real count ÷ that year's total dispositions × 100) and arrange the same three rows. Two decimals are kept; checking by hand from the displayed numbers, a cell can differ by 0.01 because of rounding.

In [5]:
# (b) Three rows per 100 dispositions: FY2008 actual -> hypothetical -> FY2025 actual
sh={y:cnt.loc[(y,'DHS'),'Share of all dispositions (%)'] for y in (2008,2025)}            # DHS dispositions per 100
rt={(y,s):cnt.loc[(y,s),'Full release (%)'] for y in (2008,2025) for s in ('DHS','Outside DHS')}
def row(dist_year,rate_year):
    dn=sh[dist_year]; on=100-dn; dr=rt[(rate_year,'DHS')]; orr=rt[(rate_year,'Outside DHS')]
    return {'DHS per 100':dn,'DHS rate (%)':dr,'Outside DHS per 100':on,'Outside DHS rate (%)':orr,
            'DHS full releases':dn*dr/100,'Outside DHS full releases':on*orr/100,'Government-wide (%)':dn*dr/100+on*orr/100}
chain=pd.DataFrame({'FY2008 actual':row(2008,2008),
                    'Hypothetical: FY2008 DHS share, FY2025 rates':row(2008,2025),
                    'FY2025 actual':row(2025,2025)}).T
display(chain.round(2))
g=chain['Government-wide (%)']
assert g.round(1).tolist()==[41.6,17.2,9.5]
assert abs(g.iloc[0]-cnt.loc[(2008,'All government'),'Full release (%)'])<1e-9 and abs(g.iloc[2]-cnt.loc[(2025,'All government'),'Full release (%)'])<1e-9
rate_eff,dist_eff=g.iloc[1]-g.iloc[0],g.iloc[2]-g.iloc[1]

  • Row 1 to row 2 (41.6% to 17.2%, down 24.4 points): the effect of the falling full-release rates of DHS and of agencies outside DHS. Outside DHS accounts for 22.7 points and DHS for 1.7, so almost all of it comes from outside DHS.
  • Row 2 to row 3 (17.2% to 9.5%, down 7.7 points): the effect of DHS's larger share of dispositions. About 42 of every 100 dispositions moved from outside DHS to DHS (DHS's share of dispositions rose from 18.9% to 60.8%); at FY2025 rates (20.70% outside DHS, 2.35% at DHS), those 42 would give 8.7 full releases outside DHS but only 1.0 at DHS.

Under this hypothetical: 32.1 points = outside DHS rate fell 22.7 + DHS rate fell 1.7 + DHS's larger share of dispositions 7.7.

(c) A different hypothetical gives different numbers; take the average

The hypothetical above combines FY2008 shares of dispositions with FY2025 rates. It can also run the other way, combining FY2025 shares with FY2008 rates. Each part is “the change in one thing × the size of the other thing,” and the result depends on which year's value the other thing takes:

  • Outside DHS rate fell = the fall in the outside-DHS rate × how many dispositions are outside DHS: 81.14 per 100 in FY2008 but only 39.15 in FY2025.
  • DHS rate fell = the fall in DHS's rate × how many dispositions are at DHS (18.86 or 60.85 per 100).
  • DHS's larger share of dispositions = the extra 41.99 per 100 closed by DHS × the gap between the outside-DHS and DHS full-release rates: 37.3 points in FY2008 but only 18.3 points in FY2025.

Both hypotheticals are reasonable. Kitagawa's method takes their average to give one set of numbers, and the two hypotheticals are reported as a range. Section 6 handles agency weights the same way (starting-year, ending-year and average weights). The table shows the three sets; the formulas for each number follow it.

Result: of the 32.1-point decline in the government-wide full-release share, about 16.8 points come from the falling rate outside DHS (10.9–22.7 under the two hypotheticals), about 11.7 points from DHS's larger share of dispositions (7.7–15.7), and about 3.6 points from DHS's own falling rate (1.7–5.5). The first two are large; DHS's own rate decline has the smallest effect.

Two limits: this is an arithmetic split that shows how many points each part accounts for, not why; and it uses only two groups, DHS and outside DHS. A different grouping changes the size of the share part (Section 6 splits by individual agency, which is another grouping).

No records: averages left blank because the DHS share effect changes sign between the two hypotheticals (−3.8 and +11.3).
  • Partial release: the government-wide partial-release share rose 20.0 points (17.8% to 37.7%): +10.1 on average from rate changes and +9.9 on average from DHS's larger share of dispositions (+2.4 to +17.4 under the two hypotheticals). The range is wide because the partial-release rates of DHS and of agencies outside DHS differed greatly in FY2008 (51.3% versus 10.0%) but much less in FY2025 (40.0% versus 34.3%).
  • No records: the share effect has opposite signs under the two hypotheticals (−3.8 and +11.3), because DHS's no-records rate was below the outside-DHS rate in FY2008 (7.9% versus 16.9%) but far above it in FY2025 (40.2% versus 13.4%). Since even its sign is uncertain, the share effect is not interpreted; only the simpler fact is stated: the no-records share outside DHS did not rise (16.9% to 13.4%), and the government-wide rise comes from DHS (7.9% to 40.2%).
  • Full exemption denial: rate changes add 1.0 point on average (DHS 1.1% to 1.5% and outside DHS 4.5% to 5.8%, both rising), but DHS's larger share of dispositions subtracts 1.6 on average (1.4 to 1.8 under the two hypotheticals), so the government-wide share falls from 3.8% to 3.2%. Check with counts: FY2008 = (1,190 + 20,890) ÷ (109,028 + 469,113) = 3.82% and FY2025 = (14,735 + 37,033) ÷ (994,992 + 640,181) = 3.17%, while DHS's own rate goes from 1.09% to 1.48% and the rate outside DHS from 4.45% to 5.78%. DHS and agencies outside DHS both rise while the government-wide share falls; this pattern is known as Simpson's paradox. It holds for the FY2008 and FY2025 endpoints, not for every pair of years.

Section 2 findings

  • Full release: of the 32.1-point decline in the government-wide full-release share, about 16.8 points come from the falling rate outside DHS, about 11.7 from DHS's larger share of dispositions, and about 3.6 from DHS's own falling rate (Kitagawa averages; 10.9–22.7, 7.7–15.7 and 1.7–5.5 under the two hypotheticals). The full-release share outside DHS itself fell from 48.7% to 20.7%, so the decline is not only an effect of DHS's growing weight.
  • No records: the rise in the government-wide no-records share comes from DHS; the no-records share outside DHS did not rise.
  • Partial release: in FY2017–25 the government-wide partial-release share barely moves (36.8% to 37.7%), hiding two opposite movements: DHS falls from 56.9% to 40.0% while the share outside DHS rises from 20.5% to 34.3%. The rise outside DHS comes mainly from VBA, which Section 5 examines.
  • Full exemption denial: DHS's rate (1.1% to 1.5%) and the rate outside DHS (4.5% to 5.8%) both rise, yet the government-wide share falls from 3.8% to 3.2%. This is not a contradiction: the government-wide share adds the counts of DHS and of agencies outside DHS before dividing, so it is an average weighted by dispositions, and more and more dispositions are at DHS, whose rate is much lower (DHS's share of dispositions 18.9% to 60.8%).

These are descriptive splits of reported totals, not tests of statistical significance: the annual reports cover all requests that agencies report, not a sample.

Where the storyline goes from here. The government-wide curves combine two different patterns. Inside DHS, the no-records share rises from 7.9% in FY2008 to 40.2% in FY2025 (most of the added no-records count is at CBP and USCIS; see the appendix) and the partial-release share falls in every year after FY2018 (60.3% to 40.0%). Outside DHS, the full-release share falls. The rest of this notebook follows only the outside-DHS pattern; the DHS pattern is kept as a separate lead, and its causes are not examined here. This is why the final finding is stated for a population outside DHS rather than for the government as a whole. The next question is: is the decline in the full-release share outside DHS driven by individual agencies?

3. Why examine NARA next?¶

Section 2 showed the full-release share outside DHS jumping from 33.2% in FY2017 to 43.4% in FY2018; without NARA it moves only from 38.0% to 40.1%. This section first shows NARA's own disposition mix each year (first chart: one bar per year, all categories adding up to 100%), then uses a four-panel chart to compare each outcome outside DHS with and without NARA (two lines per panel). The comparison stays within the outside-DHS population for two reasons: Section 2 chose to follow only the outside-DHS branch, and NARA accounts for only 0.8%–7.8% of all dispositions, so in government-wide figures its effect would be hidden by changes at DHS.

NARA itself: its most common outcome changes every few years. In FY2008–17, no records is the most common outcome every year (78% or more) and full release is under 10%; in FY2018–19 full release becomes the most common (68.1% and 71.6%) and no records falls to about 5%; in FY2020 partial release is the most common (87.1%); in FY2021 full release again (76.8%); and in FY2022–25 partial release (60.3%–82.4%). The annual reports do not show why, and this notebook does not decide whether these are reporting errors or changes in classification.

NARA's weight: NARA accounts for 1.8%–15.2% of dispositions outside DHS, with larger weights in FY2016–19 and FY2023 (11% or more), enough to put swings into the outside-DHS curves.

What separating NARA changes: mainly the swings in the middle years; the endpoints barely move.

  • Full release: outside DHS 48.7% to 20.7%; without NARA 50.0% to 21.4%; the largest gap between the two lines is 5.2 points (FY2019).
  • Partial release: 10.0% to 34.3%; without NARA 10.2% to 32.3%; largest gap 6.6 points (FY2023).
  • No records: 16.9% to 13.4%; without NARA 14.7% to 13.5%; largest gap 10.8 points (FY2017).
  • Full exemption denial: 4.5% to 5.8%; without NARA 4.6% to 6.0%; largest gap 1.1 points (FY2017).

Separating NARA therefore does not create the long-run trends; it only removes the middle-year swings that NARA brings in.

This narrows the question: How did dispositions change outside DHS and NARA? That population remains explicit in the final finding; separating NARA does not establish that its reports are erroneous.

4. Revisit the outcomes: a more specific story emerges¶

Outside DHS and NARA, recalculate the four outcome shares (full release, partial release, no records and full exemption denial) with the same denominator.

Outside DHS and NARA, from FY2008 to FY2025 the full-release share falls from 50.0% to 21.4%, the partial-release share rises from 10.2% to 32.3%, and the no-records share moves from 14.7% to 13.5%, and the full-exemption-denial share stays low (4.6%–9.5% each year; 6.0% in FY2025). The full-release share falls overall but not every year: it is roughly flat in FY2009–13 (45.5%–47.3%) and rises 2.1 points in FY2018 (38.0% to 40.1%); it falls in the other years. FY2008 is the highest point and also the year with the fewest agencies in the data (26 are missing; Section 6). Starting from FY2010 instead, the share falls from 47.0% to 21.4%, or 25.6 points. The FY2018 rise comes mainly from two units whose full-release shares were already very high and whose dispositions jumped that year: USDA's FSA (18,737 to 29,393 dispositions; 93.0% to 94.8% full release) and DOJ's EOIR (41,723 to 50,271; 72.7% to 73.6%), contributing 2.51 and 1.51 points; fewer dispositions or lower shares at units such as SSA and DOS offset part of it (see the contribution table above; the two OPM rows, +1.90 and −1.81, reflect OPM changing its component code that year from OPM/AO to OPM/OPM CO, and they largely cancel out). This is a change in the units' weights (their numbers of dispositions), with the two units' own shares nearly unchanged, unlike NARA's switches between categories.

A more specific pattern emerges: the full-release share declined while the partial-release share increased, without a corresponding long-run rise in no-records outcomes. This is a first statement; Sections 5–7 test whether individual agencies or changes in their weights drive it.

The chart and the two tables above use the same layout and years as Section 1, so each cell can be compared with the government-wide figure there. For example, the FY2025 full-release share is 9.5% government-wide but 21.4% outside DHS and NARA; the no-records share is 29.7% government-wide but 13.5% here.

These four outcomes do not cover all 12 disposition categories; the other eight are grouped as other dispositions. Before settling on that wording, look at all 12 categories every year (one bar per year, adding up to 100%), then compare the endpoints.

Outside DHS and NARA, other dispositions (the eight categories not plotted in Section 1) rose from 20.5% in FY2008 to 26.8% in FY2025 (falling first and then rising: 16.6% in FY2017, with most of the increase in recent years). Within that group, improper requests rose from 3.7% to 8.4%, duplicate requests from 1.9% to 4.3%, and other reasons from 1.5% to 3.9%; declines in the remaining categories, such as referrals to another agency, offset part of those increases. Full exemption denials also rose by about 1.4 percentage points.

The complete table sharpens the wording: the partial-release share rose 22.0 points, less than the 28.5-point fall in the full-release share, and other dispositions also changed. We therefore describe two shifts in annual totals, not a request-by-request substitution.

5. The jump in partial releases from FY2023: does one unit drive the finding?¶

In Section 4's chart, the partial-release share outside DHS and NARA stays between 21.2% and 24.4% every year in FY2014–22, then jumps from FY2023: 23.1% in FY2022, 27.9% in FY2023, 31.7% in FY2024 and 32.3% in FY2025. As with the FY2018 rise in Section 4, first break the jump down by unit (components where an agency reports them; an agency without components counts as one unit):

  • Each unit's contribution = its partial releases ÷ all dispositions outside DHS and NARA, later year minus FY2022.
  • The contributions of all units add up exactly to the change in the combined share.

The breakdown covers FY2022 to FY2023 (the year of the jump) and FY2022 to FY2025 (the last year); the unit with the largest contribution is then shown year by year.

In [11]:
# Where the jump in the partial-release share comes from: each unit's contribution =
# (its partial releases / all dispositions in the population), later year minus FY2022; contributions add up to the change
def unit_counts(y,c,base=noDN):
    n=bykey(y,c,base,COK); dp=defaultdict(float)
    for cc in c02:
        for k,v in bykey(y,cc,base,COK).items(): dp[k]+=v
    return n,dp
def contributions(c,y0,y1,base=noDN):
    (n0,dp0),(n1,dp1)=unit_counts(y0,c,base),unit_counts(y1,c,base)
    T0,T1=sum(dp0.values()),sum(dp1.values())
    return pd.Series({k:100*(n1.get(k,0)/T1-n0.get(k,0)/T0) for k in set(dp0)|set(dp1)}),(n0,dp0),(n1,dp1)

Almost all of the jump comes from VBA, the Veterans Benefits Administration within VA (the Department of Veterans Affairs).

  • FY2022 to FY2023: the combined share rises 4.77 points = VBA +8.95 + all other units combined −4.18.
  • FY2022 to FY2025: it rises 9.17 points = VBA +14.73 + all other units combined −5.56.
  • Among the other units, the largest single contribution in absolute value is only 0.53 points (FY2022–23, VA's VHA) and 0.80 points (FY2022–25, DOJ's FBI).

The other units' combined contribution is negative for two reasons. First, their own partial-release share falls (without VBA: 22.9% in FY2022, 20.6% in FY2023, 20.1% in FY2025). Second, VBA's dispositions surge, so the other units' share of all dispositions falls from 97.9% to 88.6% from FY2022 to FY2023 (100% minus VBA's 2.1% and 11.4%), and their partial releases are spread over a larger total.

VBA itself: its volume and its outcomes change at the same time. Its dispositions go from 7,586 in FY2022 to 54,244 in FY2023, 97,415 in FY2024 and 99,224 in FY2025, rising from 2.1% of all dispositions outside DHS and NARA to 11.4%, 16.8% and 16.2%. Meanwhile its partial-release share rises from 31.3% to 84.4%, 95.4% and 95.0%, and its full-release share falls from 56.0% to 11.2%, 2.3% and 1.5%. The annual reports do not show why, and this notebook does not decide whether VBA changed how it handles requests or how it reports them.

VBA's shares also swung widely in earlier years, but then it was too small to move the total. In the chart, VBA's full-release share is 75.6% in FY2008, falls to 15.1% in FY2013 and is back at 67.1% in FY2021. In FY2008–22 VBA accounts for only 0.7%–5.1% of dispositions outside DHS and NARA, so its effect on the total is small; from FY2023 it accounts for 11.4%–16.8%, enough to move it.

The next test: with VBA this large, check whether Section 4's provisional finding holds without it. Remove VBA from all years and recalculate the shares outside DHS and NARA, first for the full-release decline and then for the partial-release rise.

With VBA removed from all years, the full-release share outside DHS and NARA still falls from 48.6% in FY2008 to 25.3% in FY2025, a drop of 23.3 points; with VBA it falls from 50.0% to 21.4%, a drop of 28.5 points. VBA does not account for the full-release decline; including it only makes the decline larger.

Without VBA, the line rises once more, in FY2023 (29.6% to 32.1%). Broken down by unit (as in Section 4, with VBA removed from the population), the FY2022–23 change of +2.5 points = DOJ's EOIR (the immigration courts) +7.7 + all other units combined −5.2. EOIR's dispositions rose from 46,172 to 104,290 that year and its full-release share from 47.2% to 56.3%. The share falls again in FY2024–25.

Now test the other half: the rise in partial releases. VBA's change is concentrated from FY2023 on, so comparing only FY2008 and FY2025 would mix the change before VBA's shift with the change VBA brings. Split the 18 years at FY2017 into two periods of similar length: FY2008–17 is unaffected by VBA's shift, and FY2017–25 contains it (Section 6 uses the same split). The table compares how the complete outcome mix changes in each period in three populations: outside DHS and NARA; also without VBA; and also without all of VA, VBA's parent agency (to see whether other VA components have a similar effect).

In FY2008–17, in all three populations (outside DHS and NARA; also without VBA; also without all of VA), the decline in the full-release share is matched mainly by a rise in the partial-release share (for example, without VBA: full release −10.6 points, partial release +12.3 points).

FY2017–25 differs. Outside DHS and NARA, the partial-release share rises 9.0 points, but falls 2.8 points without VBA (22.9% to 20.1%) and 2.7 points without VA. Without VBA, the 12.7-point decline in the full-release share is matched mainly by a rise in other dispositions (+14.9 points); the no-records share rises 2.1 points. In FY2024–25, VBA accounts for about half of all partial releases outside DHS and NARA.

A single-unit removal drops one agency or component from all years; there are 571 of them here (for an agency without components, removing the agency and removing its only component are the same thing, so it counts once). Only removing VBA or all of VA turns the FY2017–25 change in the partial-release share negative; every other removal leaves a rise of at least 8.2 points. Without VBA, the rise in other dispositions is at least 14.3 points after any further single-unit removal. The largest contributors are improper requests (+5.0), other reasons (+3.4) and duplicate requests (+3.3).

Without VBA, the rise in other dispositions is spread across many units. Breaking down the FY2017–25 change of +14.9 points by unit (as in Section 4, in the population outside DHS, NARA and VBA): the largest contributions are DOJ's EOIR (+2.2) and HHS's CMS (+1.6); the ten largest contributors together add +8.3, and all other units +6.6. No single unit drives it, consistent with the rise of at least 14.3 points after any single removal above. The annual reports do not show why it rose, and this notebook does not examine it.

A second denominator: requests whose records were reviewed. Under the definitions in Section 1, a request whose records were reviewed must be reported as a full release, a partial release or a full exemption denial; no records and the other eight categories are used only when no records were processed. Above, without VBA, the FY2017–25 fall in the full-release share was matched mainly by a rise in other dispositions. A fall in "full releases as a share of all dispositions" can therefore have two sources: fewer full releases among requests whose records were reviewed, or more requests closed without records being processed.

The second denominator, full releases ÷ (full + partial releases + full exemption denials), asks only: among requests whose records were reviewed, how many were released in full? Three populations are shown: outside DHS and NARA; also without VBA; and also without VBA and EOIR (see the FY2023 EOIR rise above).

Results:

  • Among requests whose records were reviewed, the full-release share also falls. Outside DHS and NARA: 77.2% in FY2008, 54.4% in FY2017 and 35.9% in FY2025; without VBA: 76.0%, 54.7% and 48.1%. After removing any single unit it still falls in both periods: outside DHS and NARA, by at least 19.1 points in FY2008–17 (removing HHS's CMS) and 6.5 points in FY2017–25 (removing VBA); without VBA, by at least 4.4 points in FY2017–25 (removing DoD).
  • Splitting the original share into two factors: full releases ÷ all dispositions = (reviewed requests ÷ all dispositions) × (full releases ÷ reviewed requests). Without VBA, FY2017 is 69.6% × 54.7% = 38.1% and FY2025 is 52.6% × 48.1% = 25.3%. The change splits exactly into two parts (second table above: part 1 = the change in the reviewed share × the other factor's two-year average; part 2 = the total minus part 1, from the two-decimal values shown):
    • FY2008–17: the whole decline comes from fewer full releases among reviewed requests (−14.24 without VBA); the reviewed share actually rose (64.0% to 69.6%, +3.68), softening the decline slightly.
    • FY2017–25 without VBA: the original share falls 12.74 points; 8.74 points come from the falling reviewed share (69.6% to 52.6%, i.e. more requests closed without records being processed), and only 4.00 points from fewer full releases among reviewed requests (54.7% to 48.1%).
    • FY2017–25 with VBA: the share falls 16.57 points, of which 12.00 come from fewer full releases among reviewed requests, mainly VBA's switch to partial releases.
  • EOIR props up the new denominator too: without VBA, the new share is nearly flat in FY2021–25 (49.9% to 48.1%) and rises to 54.3% in FY2023, when EOIR's dispositions doubled. Also without EOIR, FY2017–25 goes from 49.0% to 35.4%, and the only year it rises is FY2018; the two parts are then −7.38 and −8.23, about half each.
  • A fact that does not depend on the denominator: without VBA, the number of full releases fell from 147,853 in FY2017 to 129,974 in FY2025, while dispositions rose from 388,535 to 513,446.

So the FY2017–25 fall in full releases as a share of all dispositions is not only "less released among reviewed requests": without VBA, most of it (8.74 of 12.74 points) reflects more requests closed without records being processed; among reviewed requests the full-release share also fell, but by less.

Section 5 in brief:

  • The full-release decline does not depend on VBA. With VBA removed from all years, the share still falls from 48.6% to 25.3%.
  • The partial-release rise has two periods. In FY2008–17 it does not depend on VBA (still +12.3 points without it); in FY2017–25 it depends entirely on VBA (−2.8 points without it; among 571 removals, only removing VBA or all of VA does this). The choice of split year matters little: without VBA, the partial-release share is 20.9%–24.1% in every year of FY2014–22 and 18.8%–20.6% in FY2023–25.
  • Without VBA, the FY2017–25 full-release decline is matched mainly by a rise in other dispositions (+14.9 points, mostly improper requests, other reasons and duplicates), spread across many units.
  • On the reviewed-requests denominator the full-release share also falls, but less in FY2017–25: without VBA it goes from 54.7% to 48.1%; of the 12.74-point fall in the original share, 8.74 points reflect more requests closed without records being processed.
  • VBA is a separate lead in its own right: its dispositions rose from 7,586 in FY2022 to 99,224 in FY2025, and 95% or more were partial releases in FY2024–25; the cause has not been examined.

The wording therefore needs two periods: in FY2008–17, the decline in the full-release share was matched mainly by a rise in the partial-release share; in FY2017–25, the rise in the partial-release share outside DHS and NARA comes from VBA, and without VBA the full-release decline was matched mainly by a rise in other dispositions.

6. Could changes in agencies' weights explain the decline?¶

Section 2 measured how much the growth in DHS's share of dispositions affected the government-wide share. This section asks the same question agency by agency outside DHS and NARA: does the decline in the full-release share come from agencies' own full-release shares falling, or from requests shifting toward agencies that release less in full (a change in weights; an agency's weight = its dispositions ÷ all dispositions outside DHS and NARA)?

The method is the one in Step 2 of Section 2 (a composition decomposition, Kitagawa 1955), with one group per agency instead of two groups (DHS and outside DHS):

  • Within-agency change = the sum over agencies of (end-year share − start-year share) × the agency's weight. The weights come from the start year, the end year or their average, matching the two hypotheticals and the Kitagawa average in Section 2.
  • Remainder = total change − within-agency change. It contains the change in weights and the agencies with data in only one of the two years (their own change cannot be measured).

The periods follow Section 5: FY2008–17 and FY2017–25, plus the whole span FY2008–25.

FY2008 coverage is incomplete: foia.gov data (the CSV, XML and API all agree) have no FY2008 figures for 26 agencies such as USDA, EEOC, NLRB, PBGC, USPS and CIA; 3 of them (including CIA) first appear in FY2009 and 23 in FY2010, so FY2009 is incomplete as well; in FY2010 together they account for 12.2% of dispositions outside DHS and NARA. Their FY2010 full-release share (48.3%) is close to that of the other agencies (46.9%), so their absence barely moves the starting level of full releases; their partial-release share is much higher (28.8% against 14.2%), so the FY2008 partial-release share is somewhat understated. A rough check: adding them to FY2008 with their FY2010 counts gives full release 49.8% (actual 50.0%), partial release 12.2% (actual 10.2%) and no records 13.5% (actual 14.7%). Outside DHS and NARA, 68 agencies have dispositions in FY2008, 112 in FY2017 and 116 in FY2025.

# Composition decomposition outside DHS and NARA: total change = within-unit change + remainder
def fr_counts(y,key=AGK):
    n=bykey(y,FG,noDN,key); dp=defaultdict(float)
    for c in c02:
        for k,v in bykey(y,c,noDN,key).items(): dp[k]+=v
    return n,{k:v for k,v in dp.items() if v}
def decompose(y0,y1,key=AGK):
    (n0,d0),(n1,d1)=fr_counts(y0,key),fr_counts(y1,key); D0,D1=sum(d0.values()),sum(d1.values())
    ks=[k for k in d0 if k in d1]                      # units with dispositions in both years
    dr={k:n1.get(k,0)/d1[k]-n0.get(k,0)/d0[k] for k in ks}
    w={'start':pd.Series({k:100*d0[k]/D0*dr[k] for k in ks}),'end':pd.Series({k:100*d1[k]/D1*dr[k] for k in ks})}
    w['mean']=(w['start']+w['end'])/2
    total=round(100*(sum(n1.values())/D1-sum(n0.values())/D0),2)
    row={'Total change':total}
    for s in ('start','end','mean'): row[f'Within ({s}-year weights)' if s!='mean' else 'Within (mean weights)']=round(w[s].sum(),2)
    for s,lab in (('start','Within (start-year weights)'),('end','Within (end-year weights)'),('mean','Within (mean weights)')):
        row[lab.replace('Within','Remainder')]=round(total-row[lab],2)    # remainder = total minus within, from the rounded values
    cov={'Units in both years':len(ks),'Their share of start-year dispositions (%)':100*sum(d0[k] for k in ks)/D0,
         'Their share of end-year dispositions (%)':100*sum(d1[k] for k in ks)/D1}
    return row,w,cov
periods={f'FY{a}–{str(b)[2:]}':(a,b) for a,b in [(2008,2017),(2017,2025),(2008,2025)]}
dec_ag={p:decompose(*yy) for p,yy in periods.items()}
dec_co={p:decompose(*yy,key=COK) for p,yy in periods.items()}
for label,dec in (('By agency',dec_ag),('By component (agencies without components count as one unit; components matched by code)',dec_co)):
    print(label+': change in the full-release share outside DHS and NARA (percentage points)')
    display(pd.DataFrame({p:v[0] for p,v in dec.items()}).round(2))
    display(pd.DataFrame({p:v[2] for p,v in dec.items()}).T.round(1).astype({'Units in both years':int}))
tab_ag=pd.DataFrame({p:v[0] for p,v in dec_ag.items()}); tab_co=pd.DataFrame({p:v[0] for p,v in dec_co.items()})
for t in (tab_ag,tab_co):
    for s in ('start-year weights','end-year weights','mean weights'):
        assert (t.loc[f'Within ({s})']+t.loc[f'Remainder ({s})']).round(2).equals(t.loc['Total change'].round(2))

                                         [2.34,-2.72,1.20],[-6.08,-3.44,-8.05],[-1.87,-3.08,-3.42]]

late_set=set(late); in_late=lambda r:noDN(r) and AGK(r) in late_set; not_late=lambda r:noDN(r) and AGK(r) not in late_set
share10=lambda c,cond:100*tot(G,c,2010,cond)/sum(tot(G,cc,2010,cond) for cc in c02)
assert [round(share10(FG,in_late),1),round(share10(FG,not_late),1),round(share10(PG,in_late),1),round(share10(PG,not_late),1)]==[48.3,46.9,28.8,14.2]

assert [round(100*(tot(G,c,2008,noDN)+tot(G,c,2010,in_late))/(d08+d_late),1) for c in (FG,PG,NR)]==[49.8,12.2,13.5]

How to read the tables: in each column, total change = within-agency change + remainder (add the two rows that use the same weights; the remainder is calculated from the two-decimal values shown). Below each decomposition table is its coverage: how many units have data in both years and what share of each year's dispositions they account for.

FY2017–25: most of the decline comes from agencies' own shares. The total falls 16.57 points. By agency, the within-agency change is −13.85 with start-year weights, −13.13 with end-year weights and −13.49 on average, less than one point apart; the remainder is only −2.72 to −3.44. The 107 agencies with data in both years cover almost all dispositions in both years (100.0% and 99.9%).

FY2008–17: the within-agency change is also the larger part, but its size depends on the weights. The total falls 11.97 points; the within-agency change ranges from −14.31 (start-year weights) to −5.89 (end-year weights), −10.10 on average. The gap is wide because the two agencies whose full-release shares fell most also shrank sharply: VA's weight went from 21.6% to 6.4% and its share from 52.4% to 22.0%; HHS's weight from 14.6% to 8.8% and its share from 70.3% to 40.2%. With FY2008's large weights their declines count for a lot; with FY2017's small weights, for much less. Of the gap between the two weightings, VA accounts for 4.63 points and HHS for 1.77. In addition, only 68 of the 112 agencies with dispositions in FY2017 have FY2008 data; they account for 86.5% of FY2017 dispositions, and the rest can only enter the remainder.

The same decomposition by component (second table). By agency, a change in the mix of components inside an agency counts as that agency's own change. For example, VA's full-release share fell from 22.0% in FY2017 to 2.4% in FY2025 mainly because VBA's weight inside VA surged (Section 5). By component, the FY2017–25 within-unit change is −10.35 (start-year weights) to −14.20 (end-year weights), −12.28 on average, still most of the −16.57 total. The 3.85-point gap between the two weightings comes mainly from VBA (5.04 points): its weight was small in FY2017 and large in FY2025, and its full-release share fell from 35.8% to 1.5%. For FY2008–17 the component result is −15.90 to −6.80 (−11.35 on average), as weight-dependent as the agency result.

Next, which agencies contribute most to the within-agency change.

Which agencies contribute most to the within-agency change? (table above, mean weights, percentage points)

  • FY2008–17: VA −4.26, HHS −3.52 and SSA −2.33; together about −10.1, almost the same as the −10.10 for all agencies, while the other agencies' rises and falls roughly cancel. DOJ (+1.71; full-release share 33.9% to 44.1%) and DOT (+0.46; 37.9% to 53.2%) move the other way.
  • FY2017–25: VA −2.59, DoD −2.49, DOT −1.13, DOJ −1.05, HHS −1.05 and USDA −0.85; together about −9.2, about two-thirds of the −13.49 for all agencies.

The main contributors differ between the periods: in FY2008–17 the within-agency decline is concentrated in VA, HHS and SSA; in FY2017–25 it is more spread out, with DoD, DOT and DOJ also falling. The same set of agencies therefore cannot describe the whole period. The two charts above show the three FY2008–17 agencies (VA is also first in FY2017–25) and the other four FY2017–25 agencies.

Now count every agency. Outside DHS and NARA, among agencies with data in both years, how many saw their full-release share fall? Agencies are counted at the agency level, with components combined into their parent agency.

Agencies with very few dispositions have unstable shares: with 5 dispositions a year, one more full release moves the share by 20 points. The table therefore uses four minimum-size thresholds (at least 1, 10, 100 or 1,000 dispositions in both years), plus a view that needs no threshold: the share of these agencies' FY2025 dispositions handled by the agencies whose full-release share fell. An agency whose share is the same in both years (for example 0% in both) is not counted as falling.

In [18]:
# Count agencies (outside DHS and NARA) whose full-release share fell, under several minimum-size thresholds
def agency_rates(y):
    fr,dp=bykey(y,FG,noDN,AGK),defaultdict(float)
    for c in c02:
        for k,v in bykey(y,c,noDN,AGK).items(): dp[k]+=v
    return fr,dp
rates_by_year={y:agency_rates(y) for y in (2008,2017,2025)}
rows=[]
for y0,y1 in [(2017,2025),(2008,2025)]:
    (f0,d0),(f1,d1)=rates_by_year[y0],rates_by_year[y1]
    for th in (1,10,100,1000):
        ks=[k for k in d0 if k in d1 and d0[k]>=th and d1[k]>=th]
        dec=[k for k in ks if f1[k]/d1[k]<f0[k]/d0[k]]
        rows.append({'Period':f'FY{y0}–{str(y1)[2:]}','Minimum dispositions in both years':th,
                     'Agencies compared':len(ks),'Agencies whose full-release share fell':len(dec),
                     'Share of agencies (%)':100*len(dec)/len(ks),
                     'Their share of these agencies\' FY2025 dispositions (%)':100*sum(d1[k] for k in dec)/sum(d1[k] for k in ks)})
counts=pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index(['Period','Minimum dispositions in both years'])
display(counts.round(0).astype(int))
assert counts[['Agencies compared','Agencies whose full-release share fell']].astype(int).values.tolist()==[[107,87],[94,77],[54,49],[26,24],[67,57],[64,56],[36,32],[20,18]]

  • FY2017–25: with no threshold (at least 1 disposition), 87 of the 107 agencies with data in both years saw their full-release share fall (81%); the share rises with the threshold, to 24 of 26 (92%) at 1,000 or more. By dispositions, the agencies whose share fell handled 96%–97% of these agencies' dispositions under all four thresholds.
  • FY2008–25: 57 of 67 with no threshold (85%) and 18 of 20 at 1,000 or more (90%). By dispositions the figure is only 70%–71%, because DOJ, the agency outside DHS and NARA with the most dispositions in FY2025, saw its full-release share rise over this period (33.9% to 39.3%); DOJ did fall during FY2017–25 (44.1% to 39.3%).
  • Why DOJ's total rose: the mix inside DOJ changed (last table above). EOIR's share of DOJ dispositions rose from 22.2% in FY2008 to 63.3% in FY2025 while its own full-release share fell from 71.3% to 56.9%; the rest of DOJ fell from 23.2% to 8.8%. Both parts fell, yet the total rose from 33.9% to 39.3%, because EOIR, with its high full-release share, carried more and more weight. This is the same kind of Simpson's paradox as the full exemption denials in Section 2; Section 7 shows EOIR also propping up the total outside DHS and NARA.
  • On the reviewed-requests denominator (Section 5): in FY2017–25, 69%–86% of agencies saw their share fall depending on the threshold (74 of 107 with no threshold; 32 of 41 with at least 100 reviewed requests in both years), or 76% by volume, lower than on the original denominator (81%–92% and 96%–97%); agencies whose share rose include DOJ (72.6% to 77.3%) and DOL (15.5% to 28.8%). For FY2008–25 it is 82%–87%, or 75% by volume. Most agencies still fall, but less one-sidedly.
  • The finding does not depend on the threshold: however the agencies are counted, most of them saw their full-release share fall. All versions are listed; which one to use externally is left to the client.

Now count by component. The counts above are by agency; does the same hold at the component level? Agencies with components are counted component by component; agencies without components count as one unit. Components are matched across years by code, so units that were renamed, merged or split cannot be matched and are left out: outside DHS and NARA there are 431 units in FY2017 and 382 in FY2025, of which 350 match (337 in FY2008, of which 239 match FY2025). The thresholds are the same as above.

In [19]:
# The same count at component level: components of an agency count separately; agencies without components count as one unit
def unit_rates(y):
    fr,dp=bykey(y,FG,noDN,COK),defaultdict(float)
    for c in c02:
        for k,v in bykey(y,c,noDN,COK).items(): dp[k]+=v
    return fr,dp

Section 6 in brief:

  • The FY2017–25 decline comes mainly from agencies' own shares falling, not from requests shifting toward agencies that release less: the total is −16.57 points; the within-agency change is −13.13 to −13.85 by agency and −10.35 to −14.20 by component.
  • In FY2008–17 the within-agency change is the larger part with start-year and mean weights, but less than half with end-year weights (−14.31, −10.10 and −5.89 by agency, against a total of −11.97); it comes mainly from VA, HHS and SSA, and this period is also affected by the 26 agencies missing from the FY2008 data.
  • Most units are falling: in FY2017–25, 81%–92% of agencies and 82%–85% of components, or 91%–97% by dispositions. On the reviewed-requests denominator, 69%–86% of agencies, or 76% by volume.
  • DOJ is the exception, because of its internal mix: DOJ's total rose over FY2008–25, but EOIR and the rest of DOJ both fell.

7. Final checks: does the finding depend on any single unit or on the list of agencies?¶

The earlier sections followed up anomalies as they appeared (NARA, the FY2018 rise, VBA, EOIR). This section checks systematically:

  • Single-unit removal: remove one agency or one component at a time (571 removals: 126 agencies and 445 components; for the 95 agencies without components, removing the agency and removing its only component are the same thing, so each counts once) from all years, with DHS and NARA still excluded. For each of the four outcomes, check whether the change over FY2008–17, FY2017–25 and the whole span FY2008–25 reverses direction, and find the smallest and largest change. Not every year has to fall; individual years tick up, for example by 2.1 points in FY2018.
  • A fixed list of agencies: recalculate with only the agencies that have data in all 18 years (end of this section).
In [20]:
sens=distinct(pd.DataFrame({str(k):v for k,v in paired([FG],c02,noDN).items()}))
print('Distinct single-unit removals:',sens.shape[1]-1)

loo={o:distinct(pd.DataFrame({str(k):v for k,v in paired([c],c02,noDN).items()})) for o,c in outcomes}

Single-unit removal results (first table above):

  • Full release: none of the 571 removals stops the decline in any period. The smallest declines: removing HHS's CMS in FY2008–17 (still −8.0 points), removing VBA in FY2017–25 (still −12.7) and removing all of VA over FY2008–25 (still −23.1). With FY2024 as the end year (FY2025 has no later report to compare with yet), over FY2008–24 the full-release share still falls at least 19.6 points, the partial-release share still rises at least 6.1 points, and the no-records change ranges from −2.7 to +0.9 points.
  • Partial release: the FY2008–17 rise holds under every removal, by at least 9.9 points (removing all of VA); in FY2017–25 only removing VBA or all of VA turns it into a fall (Section 5).
  • No records: the FY2008–25 change ranges from −2.9 to +1.0 points (−1.2 with no removal); the largest rise is 1.0 point (removing all of VA), so no removal produces a rise comparable to the full-release decline.
  • Full exemption denial: not part of the main story; it rises 3.9 points in FY2008–17 and falls 2.5 points in FY2017–25, and no removal reverses either direction.

A unit pulling the other way: EOIR props up the full-release share. Among the removals, the largest declines come from removing all of DOJ (36.7 points) and DOJ's EOIR, the immigration courts (34.3 points), both larger than the 28.5 points with no removal. EOIR's own full-release share has been high (69.3%–74.7% each year in FY2008–20, 47.2%–56.9% in FY2021–25), and its share of all dispositions outside DHS and NARA rose from 3.0% in FY2008 to 21.9% in FY2023 (15.3% in FY2025). As a unit with a high full-release share grows, it lifts the combined share and makes the decline look smaller. The FY2018 rise in Section 4 (EOIR contributes 1.51 points; dispositions 41,723 to 50,271) and the FY2023 rise without VBA in Section 5 (EOIR contributes 7.7 points; dispositions 46,172 to 104,290) both fall in years when EOIR's dispositions jumped.

The comparison table above puts VBA and EOIR side by side: VBA makes the full-release decline larger, EOIR makes it smaller, and the decline remains when either or both are removed. The direction of the partial-release change depends only on VBA: removing VBA turns the FY2017–25 change negative; removing only EOIR does not.

Note: Storyline 4 excludes EOIR as an immigration-related unit; Storyline 1 removes only DHS and NARA, so EOIR is included here.

A fixed list of agencies: foia.gov data lack 26 agencies in FY2008 (Section 6), so the list of agencies differs by year. Using only the 67 agencies with dispositions in all 18 years, the full-release share goes from 50.0% in FY2008 to 37.5% in FY2017 and 20.7% in FY2025, almost the same as the 50.0%, 38.0% and 21.4% for all agencies; these 67 agencies account for 83.5%–90.6% of dispositions outside DHS and NARA in each year from FY2010 to FY2025. The changing list does not affect the finding.

Section 7 in brief: the trends in all four outcomes have been checked against the removal of any single agency or component (the Section 6 decomposition and counts were not). The full-release decline in both periods, the FY2008–17 partial-release rise and the absence of a long-run rise in no-records outcomes do not depend on any single unit or on the changing list of agencies. Only the FY2017–25 partial-release rise depends on VBA, so that statement needs its own qualification. EOIR pulls the other way: removing it makes the full-release decline larger.

8. The resulting story¶

In one sentence: outside DHS and NARA, full releases fell from 50.0% of dispositions in FY2008 to 21.4% in FY2025; the decline remains after removing any single agency or component, and it comes mainly from agencies' own full-release shares falling, not from a shift in which agencies handle requests. Within that fall, in FY2017–25 without VBA most reflects more requests closed without records being processed (8.74 of 12.74 points); among requests whose records were reviewed, the full-release share also fell, but by less (54.7% to 48.1%).

In more detail:

  1. Government-wide context (Section 2): the government-wide full-release share fell from 41.6% to 9.5%, a drop of 32.1 points. About 16.8 points come from agencies outside DHS releasing in full less often, about 11.7 points only from DHS's share of dispositions growing (18.9% to 60.8%), and about 3.6 points from DHS's own share falling (Kitagawa averages). The single government-wide figure would count DHS's growing weight as "agencies releasing less", so the story is told outside DHS and NARA. NARA is set aside because its outcome categories swap wholesale every few years (Section 3).
  2. The full-release decline holds in both periods (Sections 4 and 7): outside DHS and NARA, the share falls 12.0 points in FY2008–17 and 16.6 points in FY2017–25. After removing any single agency or component (571 removals), it still falls at least 8.0 and 12.7 points in the two periods, and at least 23.1 points over the whole span. With only the 67 agencies that have data in all 18 years, it goes from 50.0% to 20.7%.
  3. Agencies' own shares fell, and the decline is broad (Section 6): of the 16.57-point fall in FY2017–25, the within-agency change is about 13.49 points (13.13–13.85 under the three weightings). In this period, depending on the threshold, 81%–92% of agencies and 82%–85% of components saw their own full-release share fall, or 91%–97% by dispositions; on the reviewed-requests denominator it is 69%–86% of agencies, or 76% by volume (Sections 5 and 6). FY2008–17 is also mainly a within-agency change, but it comes mostly from VA, HHS and SSA, and its size depends on which year's weights are used.
  4. What replaced full releases differs by period (Sections 5 and 7):
    • FY2008–17: mainly partial releases, up 13.1 points; at least 9.9 points after removing any single unit.
    • FY2017–25: the combined partial-release share rises 9.0 points, but only because of VBA. Without VBA it falls 2.8 points, and the full-release decline is matched by a 14.9-point rise in other dispositions (mainly improper requests, other reasons and duplicates, spread across many units). Put another way: without VBA, requests whose records were reviewed fell from 69.6% to 52.6% of dispositions, which accounts for 8.74 of the 12.74-point fall in the full-release share (Section 5).
  5. No-records outcomes did not rise with it (Sections 4 and 7): outside DHS and NARA, the no-records share changes −1.2 points over FY2008–25; after removing any single unit, the change ranges from −2.9 to +1.0 points.

What not to say:

  • Do not attribute the whole government-wide decline to agencies releasing less: about 11.7 points reflect DHS's growing weight.
  • Do not say partial releases have been rising in recent years without mentioning VBA.
  • Do not read the whole FY2017–25 fall in the full-release share as "agencies released less of what they reviewed": without VBA, most of it reflects more requests closed without records being processed (the reviewed share fell from 69.6% to 52.6%).
  • Do not state causes: the annual reports show that agencies' own shares fell, not whether request types, exemption use or reporting practices changed.
  • Do not treat FY2008's 50.0% as covering all agencies: 26 agencies are missing from the FY2008 data.

Leads to follow up separately:

  • The rise in DHS no-records outcomes, mainly from CBP and USCIS (Appendix).
  • NARA's wholesale swaps between outcome categories (Section 3).
  • VBA's switch to almost entirely partial releases from FY2023 (Section 5).
  • EOIR's growing weight, which props up the total outside DHS and NARA (Section 7; Storyline 4 treats it as an immigration-related unit).
  • The broad rise in other dispositions without VBA in FY2017–25 (Section 5).

Methods and remaining questions¶

  • Annual shares do not track individual requests or measure pages disclosed. A rise in partial releases does not establish that the same requests moved from full to partial release.
  • DHS/NARA exclusions separate trajectories; the finding applies to the stated population. Their own patterns remain important analytical subjects.
  • foia.gov data have no FY2008 figures for 26 agencies such as USDA and EEOC (they appear from FY2009–10), so FY2008 shares cover only the 68 agencies with data that year; Section 7 recalculates with the 67 agencies present in all 18 years, and the finding is unchanged.
  • FY2025 has no later report to compare with yet; Section 7 also checks FY2024 as the end year.
  • All figures are self-reported by agencies; NARA and VBA show that classification practices can change.
  • Why other dispositions rose outside VBA after FY2017 is not examined here; Section 5 shows only that the rise is spread across many units (largest: EOIR +2.2 and CMS +1.6; the top ten together +8.3, all others +6.6).
  • The causes of the NARA, DHS, VBA and EOIR changes remain unverified. This analysis does not attribute them to reporting practices, request types or willingness to disclose.
  • Both kinds of breakdown are arithmetic identities and descriptive tools. The composition decompositions in Sections 2 and 6 (Kitagawa 1955) depend on the grouping and on which year's weights are used, so both hypotheticals and their average are reported. The unit contributions in Sections 4 and 5 (each unit's count ÷ all dispositions, later year minus earlier year) add up exactly to the change in the total.
  • Single-unit removal drops one unit at a time (571 removals, from all years); VBA and EOIR were also removed together, but other combinations of several units were not tested. Removal checks and breakdowns are descriptive checks, not causal identification.
  • Blank cells count as 0 in totals and nothing is imputed: of the 7,348 rows outside DHS and NARA, 125 have blank disposition cells in Table 02, and 116 of these are blank in all 12 categories. Components are matched across years by code, so units that were renamed, merged or split do not match: they are left out of the component counts in Section 6 and treated as separate units in the removal checks.

Data and reproduction¶

Source: component_api_1106/component_master_no_03_06_11.csv. Disposition categories come from Table 02. Government aggregation retains component and no-component rows, plus agency-overall rows where component rows do not exist; Exclude and second-entry rows are omitted. Shared functions, including the weight decomposition, are in storyline_lib.py.

Method reference: Kitagawa, E. M. (1955). Components of a difference between two rates. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 50(272), 1168–1194.

Discovery and verification records are internal working notes (not included). Charts and tables are recalculated in this notebook.

Appendix: a first breakdown of the DHS lead¶

When the storyline branches in Section 2, the DHS lead is kept separate and the main line does not use it. This appendix gives a first breakdown that can be lifted out directly for a separate DHS analysis.

Step 1 of Section 2 showed DHS's no-records share rising from 7.9% in FY2008 to 40.2% in FY2025. First see which units account for the increase in no-records counts, then the no-records shares of those units and of DHS as a whole. The table and chart show the four units with the largest increases in no-records counts; all other units together account for under 1%.

In [21]:

DHS's no-records outcomes come mainly from CBP and USCIS. From FY2021 to FY2025, DHS's no-records count rose from 122,389 to 400,392; of the increase, CBP accounts for 47.1%, USCIS for 39.0%, ICE for 10.0% and PRIV (the DHS Privacy Office) for 3.5%. Measured from FY2008, CBP (42.5%) and USCIS (38.5%) also lead, followed by PRIV (11.0%) and ICE (8.0%). The units differ: at CBP the no-records share jumped (40.5% to 72.2%); at USCIS the share rose less (19.0% to 27.1%) but dispositions more than doubled (251,289 to 574,797). ICE's share rose the most (7.8% to 39.9%; 46.2% in FY2024), but its volume is smaller, so it accounts for 10.0% of the increase; PRIV's share stayed below 13% through FY2018, jumped to 30.7% in FY2019 (from 5.7% in FY2018), and did not rise further from FY2021 to FY2025 (46.8% to 43.8%). For DHS as a whole, the no-records share rose from 26.2% to 40.2%. The causes have not been examined.
